name: Aisha Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens in an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aisha, 43, and I operate a drill at the large mine near town. I check the coupling, set up at the face, listen as the bit moves, and write down what the rock and gauges tell me; I like catching a problem before it becomes a lost shift. Dust in the cab and late maintenance calls wear me out. My partner Jules works reception at a clinic, and our two children are in school while we pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drilling crew a quicker maintenance form would be useful if it gets a mechanic to a worn bit sooner. I have used an AI tool now and then to tidy an email, but the drill still needs someone listening at the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This sounds close to what we already have, and both wages feel secure for now. My partner Jules works at a clinic reception desk, and our four-month reserve means a small bill or a quiet week will not knock us over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the drill and reporting bit wear on the shift sheet. In the first year I'd ask the mechanic whether the new form carries the same vibration readings, then keep using it if the readings arrive intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a little saved time. I do not want a neat form to hide a bad sound, but that is something I can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bad sound do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit can chatter against a hard band before the gauge shows trouble. I stopped a run last month and the mechanic found a loose coupling, so I trust both my ears and the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Jules see any change in the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly less time copying appointments from one screen to another. Jules still has patients asking for help at the desk, and neither of us sees a pay cut in this picture.

say: I would welcome **faster maintenance forms** if they preserve readings.
I would say the **drill still needs** an operator listening at the face.
think: I expect **both wages** to remain secure under a plateau.
Our **four-month reserve** can handle a small bill.
do: Keep running the **drill** and recording bit wear on each shift.
Check new forms against **vibration readings** with the mechanic.
S0.quote: A bit can chatter against a hard band before the gauge shows trouble.
fieldNote: Aisha treats **sound and readings** as complementary safety evidence from the drill.
The household’s **four-month reserve** and stable current wages support her calm response to minor change.

steps.text: Keep running the drill and recording bit wear on shift sheets
Check new maintenance form readings with the mechanic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the clinic desk and the mine's ordering office will feel this before the drill crews. I would ask our union to get the new scheduling rules in writing, because fewer clerks should not mean unrecorded safety calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine Jules losing clinic hours when booking moves to software, even if my drill shifts stay. Four months of expenses buys time to argue or look elsewhere, but it does not make a smaller household wage painless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Jules to compare three clinic payslips as booking changes, and I'd bring any mine scheduling change to our union rep. In the first year I'd try the mine's new drilling schedule after another operator tests it, then keep a written record when it misses a safety stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy for Jules and a bit angry that software savings usually appear in workers' hours first. I still feel able to do something with our records and the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jules do with fewer hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules would ask the clinic for patient-facing shifts before applying elsewhere. I would not decide that for my partner, but we have talked about how much of the mortgage one wage can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you to use the schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want another operator to show it handles a stopped drill and a delayed mechanic without calling us idle. A good demonstration on a real shift means more to me than a slide deck.

say: I would say **clinic booking** and mine ordering change before drilling.
I would seek **written scheduling rules** through our union.
think: I fear Jules could lose **clinic hours** as booking moves online.
Our **reserve** buys time but cannot erase a pay cut.
do: Compare Jules’s **three payslips** as booking changes.
Bring mine **schedule changes** to the union representative.
Try the **drill schedule** after a proven operator test.
feel: **Uneasy** for Jules, but able to act.
S1.quote: Four months of expenses buys time to argue or look elsewhere, but it does not make a smaller household wage painless.
fieldNote: Aisha sees **Jules’s desk work** as more immediately exposed than her drill work.
She wants **hours and safety stops** before accepting new scheduling rules, and prefers a real operator test.

steps.text: Compare three clinic payslips with Jules as booking changes
Bring mine scheduling changes to the union representative
Try new drill schedule after another operator tests it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could take over clinic booking and mine planning, while capable drilling robots might come around 2031. I would ask the clinic and mine for separate staffing plans, because our household has wages in both places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules's reception job could go at the thinking AI date, and I expect many drill shifts to go when robots can work the face three years later. We have four months saved, not enough to bridge both losses, and I would be awake over the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go with Jules to the clinic staff meeting this month if partners can attend, and I'd ask our mine union for a robot staffing timetable. In 2029 I'd keep drilling while applying for a posted safety-inspection role at a nearby mine; Jules would apply for a patient-support job if reception hours were cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by two clocks ticking in one household. I can drive to another mine, but I cannot promise it will still have an opening when I need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the clinic meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which patient calls a machine handles and whether Jules can move to in-person support. We would need an answer about paid hours, not just a claim that patients will still be served.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the drill before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written offer with similar pay. The children are in school and the mortgage is due every month, so I cannot trade a real shift for a possible inspection job.

say: I would name **2028 desk AI** and drilling robots around 2031 separately.
I would demand **two staffing plans** for our household.
think: I expect Jules’s **reception work** to shrink first.
I expect many **drill shifts** to disappear later, beyond our reserve.
do: Ask the **mine union** for a robot staffing timetable.
Apply for a **safety-inspection vacancy** in 2029 if posted.
Help Jules seek **patient-support work** if hours fall.
S2.quote: We have four months saved, not enough to bridge both losses, and I would be awake over the mortgage.
fieldNote: Aisha maps **two AGI dates** onto different earners in one household.
She would seek **written offers** before leaving the drill, despite having some nearby mining options.

steps.text: Ask mine union for a written robot staffing timetable
Apply for posted safety-inspection role at a nearby mine in 2029
Help Jules apply for patient-support work if reception hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years before full thinking AI gives clinics time to protect patient support work and mines time to plan for drilling robots around 2034. I would want paid retraining written into both employers' plans, not just advice to be flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I could build a larger cushion before clinic booking changes in 2031. My drill wage may last until around 2034, but there is no guarantee a safety-inspection vacancy will wait for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine's training office this winter for the fees and hours of its safety certificate. I'd enrol if the mine pays and keeps my shifts; in 2032 I'd remain on the drill and apply for a posted inspection placement while Jules asks the clinic about patient-support training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to plan because one wage may continue while the other changes. I still worry about being sold an unpaid course as a solution to a paid job disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What certificate would matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine asks for a formal inspection certificate to sign off drill-face checks. I have a vocational certificate for operating, so I would need the added course and supervised hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can the children do during courses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I can trade school pickups while one of us studies, but we cannot both do evening classes every night. Our daughter already needs help with reading, and I intend to be there.

say: I would seek **paid retraining** before 2031 AI and 2034 robots.
I would protect **patient support** at the clinic.
think: We could strengthen our **cushion** before Jules’s booking work changes.
I cannot assume an **inspection vacancy** will remain open.
do: Ask for **safety-course fees** and hours this winter.
Apply for a **posted inspection placement** in 2032.
feel: **More capable** of planning, wary of unpaid courses.
S3.quote: I still worry about being sold an unpaid course as a solution to a paid job disappearing.
fieldNote: Aisha uses the **longer gap** to sequence training across two earners.
Her own qualification requires **supervised hours**, and she conditions enrolment on pay and continued shifts.

steps.text: Keep paid drill shifts while inspection applications are pending in 2032
Enrol in safety certificate if mine pays and keeps shifts
Apply for posted mine inspection placement in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade before thinking AI and drilling robots around 2039 gives us time to negotiate a careful handover. The union should insist that a person remains responsible for stopping an unsafe drill, even after the machine works alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when thinking AI arrives, Jules may need different clinic work; at 56 I may need a job beyond drilling. Our children will be adults, and I hope the mortgage is smaller, but neither a pension nor a new post is assured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and ask payroll for my pension statement this year, so retirement is a number rather than a story. I'd add a fixed amount to savings each payday; in 2037 I'd check local inspection openings and their qualification rules before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less pressed by the next few years, because we have wages and time to build a reserve. The long date still matters enough for me to keep asking about safety responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pension statement change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would tell us whether stopping work at 56 is even possible, though I doubt we should assume it. Jules and I would compare it with our mortgage balance before making any promise to the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be responsible for a robot drill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named supervisor should sign the safety record, and operators should be able to stop a run. A machine cannot answer a family after someone is hurt.

say: I would use the decade to negotiate **drill safety responsibility**.
I would place **robots around 2039** after thinking AI.
think: Jules may need different **clinic work** by 2036.
I may still need **paid work** at 56, despite grown children.
do: Add a fixed amount to **savings** each payday.
feel: **Less pressed** now, still attentive to safety and future wages.
S4.quote: A machine cannot answer a family after someone is hurt.
fieldNote: Aisha does not assume **retirement at 56** or continuing school-age costs in 2039.
Her long plan joins **savings and pension facts** with a union concern about named safety responsibility.

steps.text: Keep paid drill shifts and request the actual pension statement from mine payroll
Add a fixed amount to savings from each payday
Check local inspection openings and qualification rules in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Jules could lose reception hours before drilling robots arrive in 2031. Separate staffing plans from the clinic and mine, paid safety training, and time to apply for real inspection jobs would help. A household cannot budget from one employer's promise about the other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who can stop a robot drill after it starts making a bad sound. I want a named human responsible and a clear stop control, even if the machine is faster than me.

headlineQuote: A household cannot budget from one employer's promise about the other.
portrait: Aisha is a **43-year-old drill operator** with two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months saved.
She occasionally uses **AI tools**, but checks work against gauge readings and the sound of the bit.
Her partner’s **clinic desk job** faces thinking AI before her drill faces robots.
She seeks **union plans** and paid safety training tied to real inspection jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens Jules’s reception work before Aisha’s drilling work faces robots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Separate **staffing plans**, paid safety training and actual inspection openings would help their household.
